episodesAwaitingReview.title: Reading for One Thing at a Time
The Smallest Change That Puts It Right

reviews.instructions: Read each pack below, then set verdict to "approved" or "changes_required" and record who decided and when. An approved verdict is what lets reviewStatus move to reviewed; nothing else does, and Claude may not set it.

packs.title: Word Parts: Prefixes and Suffixes
packs.rule: A base is the main part of a word. A prefix goes in front of it and a suffix goes after it, and each one changes the meaning in a way you can predict. Knowing the parts lets you work out a word you have never seen.

packs.title: What the Text Says, and What You Worked Out
packs.rule: A text tells you some things directly. Everything else you put together yourself from what it tells you. Both are useful, but they are not the same, and a good reader can always say which one an idea came from.

packs.title: Working Out What the Text Does Not Say
packs.rule: Writers leave things for you to conclude. An inference is a conclusion the details support, even though nobody wrote it down. A good inference can point to the detail it rests on; a guess cannot.

packs.title: Working Out a Word from the Sentence
packs.rule: When you meet a word you do not know, the words around it usually tell you what it means. Look for an explanation right after it, a contrast word such as but or unlike, a list of examples, or the general sense of what is happening.

reviews.instructions: Read each pack below, then set verdict to "approved" or "changes_required" and record who decided and when. An approved verdict is what lets reviewStatus move to reviewed; nothing else does, and Claude may not set it.

packs.title: Vowel Sounds and What Changes Them
packs.rule: A vowel can say its short sound or its long sound. A silent e at the end, a second vowel teaming up with it, or an r straight after it will each change which sound you hear. Knowing the patterns lets you read a word you have never seen.

packs.title: Breaking Long Words into Beats
packs.rule: Every syllable holds exactly one vowel sound, so the number of vowel sounds is the number of beats. Where a word breaks depends on how many consonants sit between the vowels, and the break usually decides whether the first vowel is long or short. In a longer word, one beat is said louder than the others: that beat carries the stress.

packs.title: Commas in a List
packs.rule: When you list three or more things, put a comma after each one except the last. Two things joined by "and" need no comma at all.

packs.title: Commas Between Parts of a Sentence
packs.rule: When a sentence starts with a part that cannot stand alone — "When the rain stopped", "Although it was late" — put a comma where that part ends. When the main part comes first, no comma is needed.

packs.title: Apostrophes: Missing Letters and Ownership
packs.rule: An apostrophe does one of two jobs. It stands in for letters that were left out (do not → don’t), or it shows ownership (the dog’s bowl). It never makes a word plural.

packs.title: Punctuating What Someone Said
packs.rule: Quotation marks go around the speaker’s exact words and nothing else. A comma separates the speech from who said it, and the end mark goes inside the closing quotation mark.

packs.title: Commas Around a Name You Are Speaking To
packs.rule: When you speak TO somebody by name, a comma separates their name from the rest. Without it the name stops being the person you are talking to and becomes part of what you are saying.

reviews.instructions: Read each pack below, then set verdict to "approved" or "changes_required" and record who decided and when. An approved verdict is what lets reviewStatus move to reviewed; nothing else does, and Claude may not set it.

packs.title: Groups of Words That Are Not Sentences
packs.rule: A sentence needs someone or something (the subject) and something happening (the predicate), and it must not leave the reader waiting. A group of words missing any of those is not a sentence yet.

packs.title: Two Sentences Run Together
packs.rule: Two complete statements cannot simply be pushed together, with a comma or with nothing. Join them with a word like "and", "but" or "so", separate them with a full stop, or use a semicolon.

packs.title: Finding the Mistake
packs.rule: Editing starts with finding. Read for one kind of mistake at a time — spelling, then punctuation, then grammar — because looking for everything at once is how errors get missed.

packs.title: Fixing It Without Breaking Something Else
packs.rule: A repair has to fix the mistake and leave the meaning alone. Change the smallest thing that puts it right, then read the whole sentence again to check nothing else broke.

reviews.describes: grammar: agreement, tense and pronoun reference
reviews.instructions: Read each pack below, then set verdict to "approved" or "changes_required" and record who decided and when. An approved verdict is what lets reviewStatus move to reviewed; nothing else does, and Claude may not set it.

packs.title: Making the Verb Match the Subject
packs.rule: A verb has to match the subject in number: one thing does, more than one thing do. The trap is that the subject is not always the noun nearest the verb.

packs.title: Keeping the Time Steady
packs.rule: Tense says when something happens. Within one piece of writing it has to stay steady: if you start in the past, stay in the past unless the meaning genuinely changes.

packs.title: Pronouns That Match What They Stand For
packs.rule: A pronoun stands in for a noun, and it has to match that noun in number. It also has to be clear which noun it stands for — if two are possible, the sentence has to be reworded.

packs.title: Showing Who Owns What
packs.rule: Ownership is shown two ways: an apostrophe on a noun (the dog’s bowl) or a possessive word that replaces one (his, her, its, their). A personal possessive pronoun (his, hers, its, ours, yours, theirs, whose) never takes an apostrophe. Words like everyone’s and someone’s are not personal pronouns, and they do take one.

packs.title: Making Words Plural
packs.rule: Most words add s. The ones worth learning are the exceptions: words ending in a hissing sound add es, words ending in a consonant and y change to ies, some f words change to ves, and a few do not change at all.

packs.title: The Different Kinds of Pronoun
packs.rule: Pronouns do different jobs. Some point (this, those), some ask (who, which), some refer back to the subject (myself, themselves), some join a description onto a noun (who, which, that), and some stand for nobody in particular (anyone, several, nothing).

reviews.describes: below-grade foundation located by the diagnostic: digraphs and clusters, counting sounds, inflectional endings, long words in chunks
reviews.instructions: Read each pack below, then set verdict to "approved" or "changes_required" and record who decided and when. An approved verdict is what lets reviewStatus move to reviewed; nothing else does, and Claude may not set it.

packs.title: Two Letters, One Sound or Two
packs.rule: A digraph is two letters that make ONE sound: sh, ch, th, wh, ph, ck and ng. A cluster is two or three consonants side by side where you still hear EVERY sound: st, bl, gr, mp, nd. Some words also hold a silent letter, like the k in knee, that makes no sound at all.

packs.title: Counting Sounds, Not Letters
packs.rule: A word is made of sounds, and the number of sounds is often not the number of letters. A digraph like sh or ck is two letters but one sound, a silent letter is no sound, and a cluster like st is two sounds. Count what you hear, then check each sound against the letters that spell it.

packs.title: Adding -ing, -ed and -es
packs.rule: Before you add an ending, look at the end of the base word. If it ends in a silent e and the ending starts with a vowel, drop the e: hope, hoping. If a short word of one syllable has one short vowel and then one consonant, double that consonant: hop, hopping. Never double w, x or y: snow, snowing; mix, mixing; play, played. If it ends in a consonant and y, usually change the y to i before -es or -ed, but keep it before -ing: carry, carries, carrying. After s, x, sh or ch, add -es rather than -s: fox, foxes.

packs.title: Reading Long Words in Chunks
packs.rule: A long word is easier to read in chunks. First look for a prefix at the front and a suffix at the end, and cover them to find the base word. Then break what is left between syllables, so each chunk has one vowel sound. Read the chunks in order and blend them into the word.
